newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish government staves off EU court challenge.
newsitem.headline: Danish government staves off EU court challenge.

text.p: Denmark's government heaved a sigh of relief on Friday when the High Court dismissed a challenge to the legality of Denmark's European Union membership that could have forced it to quit the EU or change its constitution.
But the 10 petitioners vowed to fight on with an appeal to the Supreme Court, expected to be heard later this year or early in 1998.
"We certainly shall appeal to the Supreme Court," said one of the non-partisan group's lawyers, Ole Krarup, after the panel of three High Court judges unanimously rejected their claim.
The group charges that since joining the EU in 1973 Denmark has progressively ceded national authority to European Union institutions in breach of its own constitution.
The court, bound by pre-trial decisions, limited its judgement to the actual treaty of membership and Denmark's 1993 ratification of the subsequent Maastricht treaty.

"They took absolutely no account of the creeping surrender of sovereignty and made no reference in their judgement to any of the evidence or witnesses we presented during the case," Krarup told a news conference.

The government is keen to get the case resolved once and for all, saying it will wait until the final verdict before holding a referendum on EU treaty amendments agreed earlier this month at an Amsterdam summit.

The plaintiffs have a maximum of two months to lodge their appeal and Supreme Court President Niels Pontoppidan told the Danish news agency Ritzau that the case would be heard by a plenum of nine to 15 judges "as quickly as possible".
Financial markets, which shuddered when the case went to a lower court last year, ignored Friday's verdict but both the ruling Social Democrats and the opposition were jubilant.
"Getting a verdict is important in itself but it is also good to get a legal opinion from the court and that is what we have here," Social Democrat parliamentary spokeswoman Pia Gjellerup said.
"The judgement backed up the government's evidence with arguments and did not just rattle off a decision," she added.
For once the main opposition Liberals agreed with the government.

"To my mind it is wholly inappropriate that EU opponents abuse the Danish legal system on very doubtful grounds in order to undermine a treaty that both parliament and the electorate have approved," party EU spokeswoman Charlotte Antonsen said.
Danes have been traditionally cool toward outright European integration, rejecting the Maastricht Treaty in a 1992 referendum.
But voters grudgingly approved the treaty the following year on condition that Denmark opt out of economic and monetary union and joint defence, citizenship and asylum policies.
